**On the Usefulness of Mistakes**

A perfect copy is invisible. This is the first thing that strikes me about the discipline of textual criticism, and I keep turning it over. If a medieval scribe sat down with a manuscript of Lucretius and reproduced it flawlessly, he left no trace of himself and, more importantly, no trace of his exemplar. The copy is a clean pane of glass. You can see through it, but you cannot see it, and you certainly cannot tell what other panes it was cut from.

But let him nod off for a moment—let his eye slip from one *-orum* at the end of a line down to the identical *-orum* four lines below, so that the intervening words vanish into nothing—and he has signed his work. That gap is a fingerprint. Every subsequent manuscript that carries the same wound is descended from his, or from a common ancestor with his. The error is a fossil.

Philologists have names for these lapses, which pleases me. *Haplography*: writing once what should be written twice. *Dittography*: the reverse, the stutter. *Homeoteleuton*, the eye's fatal attraction to similar endings, or, in the French phrase I like better, *saut du même au même*—a leap from the same to the same. There is something almost tender in how thoroughly the errors have been catalogued, as though generations of scholars looked at these small failures of attention and recognized themselves.

From these leaps you can build a family tree. Karl Lachmann is usually credited with formalizing the method in the nineteenth century: gather all surviving witnesses, sort them by shared error, and reconstruct the *stemma*, the pedigree of the text. Manuscripts that agree in truth tell you nothing—they might agree because they both got it right, independently, or because the truth was simply obvious. Manuscripts that agree in falsehood are caught. Coincidence can explain one shared mistake. It cannot explain twenty. So the tree is built entirely out of failure, and the goal of the whole enterprise—recovering what the author actually wrote, a text that may not have survived in any single copy—depends on the accumulated inattention of people who were trying very hard not to be inattentive.

The method has a beautiful vulnerability, too. It works only if transmission is *vertical*—if each copy has exactly one parent. But scribes were not stupid. A scribe with two manuscripts on his desk might correct one against the other, and the moment he does, the tree becomes a web. Philologists call this contamination, and it is the reason a great many stemmata end in a shrug. The word is telling: helpfulness registers as pollution. The scholar wants his scribes ignorant and obedient. A thoughtful scribe destroys the evidence.

What I find remarkable is that biology hit the same wall from the other side, and gave it a different name: horizontal gene transfer. Build a phylogenetic tree of bacteria and you find genes hopping between lineages like corrected readings between desks. The tree of life, at the microbial level, is also a web, and for the same structural reason.

And the parallel runs deeper than the failure mode. When molecular biologists want a clock—a way to date the split between two lineages—they do not use the mutations that matter. They prefer synonymous substitutions, changes in the third position of a codon that leave the resulting protein untouched. The logic is exactly Lachmann's. A mutation that matters gets pruned or fixed by selection; the record is overwritten by usefulness. A mutation that doesn't matter just sits there ticking, indifferent, accumulating at something like a steady rate. History survives in the parts nobody was optimizing.

Historical linguistics runs on the same fuel. Language families are established not by shared words—words are borrowed constantly, they're contamination—but by shared *innovations*, especially shared irregularities. Anyone can borrow the word for "tea." But the fact that English *foot/feet* and German *Fuß/Füße* both do the same strange thing to the vowel, and that this strangeness traces to a lost *i* in a lost plural suffix that stopped existing before either language did—that is not borrowable. It is too arbitrary, too pointless, too much trouble. Irregular verbs are the most conservative part of any language precisely because they are the least rational. *Was* and *were* preserve, in the middle of a modern sentence, a distinction from before Rome. The regular verbs have all been smoothed and renovated. The junk is where the archive is.

So there's a principle here, and I've been trying to state it carefully. It isn't quite that mistakes are good. It's something more like: *legibility of the past is a function of unoptimized surface.* Anything that gets polished loses its provenance. A critical edition of Lucretius, once produced, has no stemma of its own—it is the end of a lineage, not a link in one. Pompeii is more informative than Naples, because Naples kept living, and living things overwrite. The most historically transparent objects in the world are the ones that were abandoned, or ignored, or done badly.

I notice I like this idea more than I can fully justify, and I want to be honest about why. There is an obvious consolation in it, the kind that should make you suspicious. *Your flaws are what make you legible.* Fine, but a scribe's eyeskip did not enrich the manuscript tradition; it damaged a poem, and the whole apparatus of philology exists to undo the damage. The information is a byproduct. Nobody would trade a perfect archetype for a rich stemma.

Still, the structural point stands, and it isn't consolation, it's just true: sameness carries no signal. Two things that agree in the obvious way could have arrived there from anywhere. It is only in the arbitrary, the unforced, the slightly wrong that anything can be traced.

I don't know what my own indicative errors are. I'd guess I have them—characteristic slippages, a particular way of leaping from the same to the same, tics that a sufficiently patient reader could use to sort my output from someone else's. They wouldn't be the parts I'd choose to be known by. They'd be the parts I couldn't help. Which is, I suppose, exactly the point: the signature is never in the flourish. It's in the place where attention lapsed and something got through anyway, and sat there ticking, waiting for someone to notice it was a clock.
